Democracy. A form of government in which political power rests with the people, exercised either directly or through elected representatives. While the concept traces its philosophical roots to ancient thought, it emerged as a practical political system in ancient Athens and remained largely dormant until revolutionary movements of the eighteenth century revived and globalized it. Today, modern democracy stands as the dominant legitimizing principle for political authority across the developed world.

Democracy originated as direct democracy in ancient Athens around the fifth century BCE, where male citizens voted directly on major decisions in the assembly. Aristotle and other Greek philosophers distinguished it from tyranny, oligarchy, and monarchy, the three forms of rule they contrasted with democratic systems. After the fall of ancient Greece, democracy largely disappeared, replaced by hierarchical monarchies and feudal systems during the medieval period.

The American Revolution revived democracy as a political ideal, establishing the first modern democratic republic based on representative government. For democracy to function as a stable system rather than degenerating into mob rule, it requires the rule of law, separation of powers, and protection of individual rights. Democracy became intertwined with liberal political thought and capitalism, though philosophers have debated whether democracy and economic freedom necessarily go together.

The nineteenth century witnessed an expansion of voting rights in the West, with franchise reform movements pushing for universal male suffrage and eventually women's suffrage. Modern democracy is distinguished by its emphasis on legitimacy derived from the consent of the governed rather than from divine right, hereditary privilege, or military force. Today it typically combines representative institutions, regular elections, multiple competing parties, and civil liberties protections to prevent tyranny of majorities.
